extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, and readers of classical satire (Horace) interested in craft and practice
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and implied standards for composing satirical verse in the Horatian/classical tradition: choosing suitable genre, practicing diligent craftsmanship, revising, and aiming at an appropriate audience while avoiding undue imitation or dangerous targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing native and Greek styles
rubrics_metrics.description: "A piebald speech, half native and half Greek!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against an awkward hybrid of native and Attic/Greek manner: Horace recounts being cautioned when he 'tried his hand at Attic poetry' that slavish imitation of Greek models is inappropriate. The example (Quirinus' warning) suggests do not force foreign mannerisms into your own voice or pursue forms for which you lack the native aptitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a genre that suits your abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: For me, this walk of satire ... Best suits my gait: yet readily I yield To him who first set footstep on that field
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the poetic field that fits your personal capacities and temperament rather than competing in genres where others clearly excel (e.g., epic, tragic, pastoral). The poem enumerates other poets who better serve other forms, implying you should avoid trying to outdo specialists and instead work in the sphere that 'suits your gait.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise repeatedly / edit diligently
rubrics_metrics.description: "you must draw your pen Not once nor twice but o'er and o'er again Through what you've written..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision is essential: prune redundancies, 'apply the file to each excrescence that deforms his style.' The passage uses Lucilius as a hypothetical example who, given more time, 'would prune redundancies' — advising iterative editing to entice readers to return and to improve clarity and polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target a learned audience, not popular applause
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not making popular applause your cue, But looking to fit audience, although few."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim primarily to please educated, discerning readers or patrons (Maecenas, Virgil, Varius, etc.) rather than pandering to the hooting crowd. The poet states that pleasing knowledgeable friends is a successful end; avoid writing solely for mass applause or for pedantic exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select targets for satire cautiously; avoid attacking the powerful recklessly
rubrics_metrics.description: "Better do this than gall with keen lampoon Cassius the rake and Maenius the buffoon, When each one... fears for himself, and hates your bitter tongue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful whom you lampoon: attacking those who can retaliate or who are sensitive may be dangerous; choose your satirical targets with prudence and consider social/political consequences and personal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware legal/libel consequences of spiteful writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a man writes ill verses out of spite 'Gainst A or B, the sufferer may indict."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirists should be conscious of legal repercussions (libel/indictment) when verses are plainly spiteful. The text notes that a laugh from a powerful patron (e.g., Caesar) might end a case, but otherwise hostile invective can provoke legal action — assess audience/authority and tone accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain writing discipline; avoid sloth and procrastination
rubrics_metrics.description: "So seldom do you write... Stop your ears to sloth's enchanting voice, Or give up your best hopes: there lies your choice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular composition and industry are required. The poem criticizes intermittent, lazy writing habits and urges steady labor: do not delay or cultivate excuses; practice and routine produce work and reputation rather than contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligent line-crafting and hard workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: "To drill reluctant words into a line, This was Lucilius' hobby, and 'tis mine."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craftsmanship matters: poets must work words into place, shaping meter and sense with painstaking effort. The poet presents composition as a craft requiring repeated attention to micro-level phrasing and meter, and pride in the finished book as a close companion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the tone of invective in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some think in satire I'm too keen, and press The spirit of invective to excess: Some call my verses nerveless: once begin, A thousand such per day a man might spin."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a tension between being too harsh and too weak. The poet acknowledges critics who find his satire excessive and others who find it feeble, implying the value of finding a measured, effective tone rather than defaulting to brute invective or timid generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain personal voice and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: "my poor implement of mine, my pen, Shall ne'er assault one soul of living men: Like a sheathed sword, I'll carry it about, A weapon I shall never care to draw,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a personal ethical stance in satire: restraint and self-restraint can be a stylistic and moral choice. The speaker intends to use the pen defensively or as a restraint rather than as an instrument of gratuitous attack — endorsing a controlled, principled voice.
